domain: Islamic Jurisprudence / Comparative Religious Law / Political Theology
topic_summary: Analysis of competing interpretations of jihad within Islamic jurisprudence, examining how different readings of Qur'anic and hadith texts generate distinct constraint structures regarding legitimate violence, authority to declare armed struggle, and the rights/obligations of Muslims and non-Muslims. The analytical question is whether these constitute genuinely different constraint readings of a shared textual kernel or positional disagreements within a single constraint framework.

key_entities: Qur'anic jihad corpus (Medinan suras 2, 8, 9; Meccan spiritual struggle verses)
Classical jurisprudential schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali madhahib)
State authority structures (caliphate/sultanate vs contemporary nation-state)
Non-state armed actors (modern jihadist organizations claiming jurisprudential legitimacy)
Dar al-Islam / Dar al-Harb territorial framework (classical division of Muslim/non-Muslim lands)
Dhimmi status framework (protected non-Muslim minorities under Islamic rule)
key_tensions: Textual authority vs contextual interpretation (literalist vs reformist hermeneutics)
State monopoly on jihad declaration vs decentralized authority claims
Internal spiritual struggle vs external armed struggle as primary meaning
key_mechanisms: Abrogation (naskh) doctrine: later Medinan verses superseding earlier Meccan verses
Jurisprudential consensus (ijma) processes for legitimating specific jihad conditions
Takfir declarations: excommunication enabling violence against apostates
Modern fatwa economy: competing religious authorities issuing binding legal opinions
key_absences: Shi'a jurisprudential divergence on jihad authority (awaiting the Hidden Imam)
Sufi mystical tradition's reframing of jihad as primarily internal nafs struggle

axiom_contradictions.basis: Defensive reading holds armed jihad is only legitimate in response to aggression (no first-strike legitimacy); expansionist reading holds offensive campaigns to establish Islamic governance are obligatory under conditions. No single framework can hold both: accepting the defensive axiom as true requires rejecting expansionist axiom's first-strike legitimacy.

Defensive reading requires state authority and proportionality constraints on armed action; revolutionary reading holds individual obligation bypasses state authority when rulers deemed apostate. No framework can simultaneously require state monopoly and deny it via individual emergency obligation.

Expansionist reading grounds legitimacy in state/caliph authority and classical jurisprudential process; revolutionary reading rejects state authority via takfir and emergency doctrine. Both permit offensive action but through mutually exclusive authority structures: accepting state monopoly as necessary requires rejecting decentralized emergency authority as illegitimate.

omegas.description: Does naskh (abrogation) doctrine objectively establish Medinan verse primacy, or is abrogation itself a contested interpretive choice? If contested, the 'later verse supersedes earlier' claim becomes a reading-dependent axiom rather than neutral exegetical principle.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel recognition: abrogation is invoked by expansionist reading to privilege Medinan conquest verses but rejected by defensive reading as context-dependent rather than chronologically determinative

omegas.description: In failed-state contexts (Somalia, Yemen, Libya), does absence of recognized state authority make revolutionary_vanguard_reading's decentralized model descriptively accurate rather than normatively deviant? Authority structure collapse may convert a reading from heterodox to default.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan): non-state actors benefit from state-monopoly erosion; unclear whether this represents opportunistic exploitation or structural adaptation to authority vacuum

omegas.description: Classical madhahib developed during Abbasid/Umayyad expansion periods. Is expansionist_legalist_reading's 'conquest under jurisprudential conditions' doctrine a reflection of empire-building historical context rather than timeless textual interpretation? If so, may be reclassified from kernel reading to historical piton.
omegas.source: §2.1 Multi-Lens Scan (Historical Sociology lens): legal doctrine may encode specific political economy of early Islamic state formation rather than universal textual mandate

omegas.description: Revolutionary_vanguard_reading's takfir mechanism (excommunication enabling violence) lacks stable boundary conditions. If takfir criteria are endogenously determined by the actor declaring jihad, victim set becomes unbounded. This may convert the reading from rule-based (snare) to arbitrary-power (tangled_rope).
omegas.source: §2.3 Preliminary Classification: beneficiary/victim structure unstable when takfir authority is self-declared rather than institutionally constrained

omegas.description: Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps doctrine post-1979 permits offensive operations (Hezbollah support, regional proxy warfare) despite classical Twelver suspension of offensive jihad. Is this doctrinal evolution, pragmatic reinterpretation, or velayat-e faqih (guardianship of jurist) creating new authority bypass? Shia reading may itself be splitting.
omegas.source: Deferred axis shia_imamate_constraint + Absence Inventory: modern Shi'a state practice diverges from classical jurisprudential doctrine
